title: Stocking stitch mittens in DK wool
subtitle: Plain full mittens worked in the round with a 2×2 ribbed cuff.
excerpt: Full mittens in DK wool with a 2×2 ribbed cuff, a stocking stitch body, and an afterthought thumb. Sized for hand circumferences of 18, 20, and 22 cm. The natural step up from a fingerless mitt.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, 8th series (1880s), §Knitted mittens. The stocking-stitch body with ribbed cuff and round top is the most common Victorian mitten construction. Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), §Mitts and gloves, gives the same ribbed-cuff structure. Both are out of UK and EU copyright.

knitting.gaugeText: 22 sts × 30 rounds = 10 × 10 cm in stocking stitch on 3.75 mm needles, blocked.
knitting.finishedSizeText: Hand circumference 18 (20, 22) cm with 1 to 2 cm negative ease. Hand length to the top of the mitten 20 (22, 24) cm from the cast-on edge.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thumb opening made by working the thumb stitches in waste yarn during the hand, then returning to them after the hand is complete. The waste yarn is removed to expose live stitches above and below the gap, which are picked up and worked as the thumb.
A method for knitting small circumferences in the round on one long circular needle. The cable is pulled into a loop at the midpoint of the stitches, splitting them across two needle tips.
Knit two together. Insert the right needle into the front of the next two stitches as one and knit them together. A right-leaning single decrease.
Slip, slip, knit. Slip two stitches one at a time knitwise, then insert the left needle through both slipped stitches from left to right and knit them together. A left-leaning single decrease.

content.text: Full mittens in DK wool, worked in the round on magic loop, sized to fit hand circumferences of 18, 20, and 22 cm.
The construction is seamless, worked in the round using
magic loop
on a long circular needle. This keeps the palm seam-free where glove wear is heaviest. The thumb uses the
afterthought thumb

method: waste yarn marks the thumb position while the hand is on the needles, and the thumb is picked up and worked afterwards. The mitten top is closed with paired decreases over the last 8 rounds. Budget about 100 g (220 m / 240 yards) of DK yarn for both mittens. Full mittens are warmer than fingerless versions and suit outdoor use in cold weather.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: 100 g (about 220 m / 240 yards) of DK-weight wool
items.substitutions: Any DK-weight wool or wool blend. A wool content of at least 50% keeps the mitten its shape after washing.

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 3.75 mm (UK 9 / US 5) circular needle, at least 80 cm cable, for magic loop

items.name: Stitch markers
items.qty: 2 — one for the beginning of the round, one to mark the thumb position

items.name: Waste yarn
items.qty: About 40 cm of smooth contrasting yarn for the afterthought thumb marker

content.text: Gauge
22 stitches and 30 rounds to 10 cm over stocking stitch on 3.75 mm needles, blocked. Knit a flat swatch of at least 25 stitches and 30 rows in stocking stitch. Block it before measuring.

If your gauge is 23 stitches per 10 cm rather than 22, the size M mitten will be about 1 cm narrower at the palm. For a 20 cm hand, that is still wearable, but a tight fit. Move up to 4 mm needles and try again if needed.
Stitches used

items.name: k2, p2
items.qty: 2×2 rib: knit two, purl two, repeated across

content.text: Pattern
Before you cast on, circle your size. Every stitch count and measurement reads S (M, L).
Cast on and cuff

Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 36 (40, 44) stitches. For the size L cast-on of 44 stitches at 3.75 mm needles, pull off about 32 cm as the tail before starting. The formula is tail_cm = (needle size in mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15.
Divide the stitches evenly across the two needle tips (18, 20, 22 per tip). Join to work in the round, placing the beginning-of-round marker.
Work 2×2 rib (k2, p2 every round) for 24 (26, 28) rounds. The cuff measures about 8 (9, 9.5) cm.
Hand to thumb position
Switch to stocking stitch (knit every round) and work for 10 (12, 14) rounds.
Thumb marker

For a right mitt, the thumb sits at the beginning of the round. Knit the first 9 (10, 11) stitches with a length of smooth waste yarn, then slip those stitches back to the left needle and knit them again with the main yarn. The waste yarn marks the thumb opening but does not change the stitch count. Continue in stocking stitch to the end of the round.
Hand above the thumb
Work in stocking stitch for a further 14 (16, 18) rounds. The mitten body from the cast-on edge measures about 18 (20, 22) cm.
Mitten top shaping
Place 4 decrease markers evenly spaced around the 36 (40, 44) stitches: markers at stitches 1, 10 (11, 12), 19 (21, 23), and 28 (31, 34).
Decrease round: *k1,
ssk
, knit to 3 stitches before next marker,
k2tog
, k1, SM*; repeat for all 4 sections. 8 stitches decreased each decrease round.
Work 1 plain round between each decrease round. Repeat until 8 stitches remain. Cut yarn, draw through all 8 stitches and pull tight to close.
Stitch count check-in after gusset: you should have 36 (40, 44) stitches before the top shaping begins. If the count is short, check the thumb marker round for a dropped stitch.
Thumb
Remove the waste yarn from the thumb gap, picking up 9 (10, 11) live stitches above and 9 (10, 11) live stitches below the gap. Total: 18 (20, 22) stitches.

Join the yarn and work 10 (12, 12) rounds of stocking stitch. If you see a small hole at each corner of the gap, pick up one extra stitch at each corner and decrease them away on the first thumb round.
Work a simple decrease round: (k1, k2tog) across. 12 (14, 15) stitches remain. Work another decrease round if needed to reduce to about 8 stitches, then cut yarn and draw through to close.
Stitch count check-in on the thumb: you should have 18 (20, 22) stitches after picking up around the thumb gap. A 2-stitch shortfall usually means a corner stitch was missed.
Mirror your second mitt

Work the second mitt to the thumb-marker round. Place the waste yarn across the last 9 (10, 11) stitches of the round instead of the first 9 (10, 11). Hold the first mitt palm-out: the thumb sits on your right. The second mitt's thumb should sit on your left. If both thumbs are on the same side, you have two right mittens.
Common faults
Two mittens for the same hand: check the thumb position before starting the second mitt. The waste yarn sits at opposite ends of the round on left and right mittens.
Cuff sags after one wash: the cast-on edge was worked looser than the body. Match your body tension when casting on, or use German twisted cast-on for extra stretch and recovery.
Top puckers instead of closing flat: the decrease markers were not spaced evenly around the round. Re-space before starting the decrease rounds if the count does not divide evenly by 4.
Holes at the thumb corners: pick up one extra stitch at each corner of the gap and k2tog with the adjacent stitch on the first thumb round.
Finishing
Weave all yarn tails in on the wrong side. The palm and thumb area take the most wear, so thread each tail through at least 5 cm of fabric in two directions.
Wet-block if using wool: soak in cool water, squeeze out without wringing, lay flat and ease to the stated measurements. Air dry before wearing.
Care
Wool: hand wash in cool water with a wool-safe detergent, or machine-wash on a delicate cycle at 30 degrees if the yarn label permits. Lay flat to dry.
Wool-acrylic blends: follow the yarn label. Most blends are hand-wash safe at 30 degrees.
What to try next

A natural step from these plain mittens is adding a gusseted thumb, which gives a better anatomical fit. From there, a two-colour Selbu-style mitten uses exactly the same top shaping with a stranded colourwork body.
